subject: Culture
title: Secondhand Clothing Flows
description: A short lesson to help you apply Secondhand Clothing Flows.

hook.text: Your donated T-shirt likely ends up in a Ghanaian market called Kantamanto, where 15 million garments arrive weekly.

buildup.text: Rich nations export used clothes to Africa and Asia. It's framed as charity but operates as a $4 billion industry.

discovery.text: East African nations tried banning used clothing imports to protect local textile jobs. The US threatened sanctions.

twist.text: Much of what arrives is unsellable. Ghana's beaches are now clogged with textile waste from the Global North.

climax.text: The secondhand chain reveals the true lifecycle: buy cheap, wear briefly, donate guiltlessly, pollute elsewhere.

punchline.text: Charity is sometimes just outsourcing your trash.

quiz.question: How many garments arrive at Ghana's Kantamanto market weekly?

details.summary: Donated clothes from wealthy nations flood developing countries, creating complex economic ripple effects. What begins as charity can devastate local textile industries — used clothing from America and Europe now dominates markets across Africa, displacing local producers.
details.whyItMatters: The secondhand clothing trade reveals how charitable intentions can produce unintended consequences, disrupting local economies while assuaging donor guilt.
takeaways: The global used clothing trade is worth over $4 billion annually
East Africa imports massive volumes of secondhand Western clothing
Rwanda banned used clothing imports to protect local industry

faq.question: Where do donated clothes actually end up?
faq.answer: Only about 10-20% of donated clothes are resold in the donor country's thrift stores. The rest are sorted and exported — the best items go to Eastern Europe, mid-quality to Africa and South America, and the lowest quality becomes industrial rags or recycled fiber.

faq.question: Why did some African countries ban used clothing imports?
faq.answer: Rwanda, Uganda, and Tanzania proposed bans because cheap imported clothes were destroying local textile and fashion industries. Rwanda followed through despite US trade threats. Leaders argued that economic independence requires the ability to clothe one's own population.
